title: 75th Anniversary Introduction
text: 75TH ANNIVERSARY INTRODUCTION Most of us first encountered George Orwell’s work as adolescents when we were assigned his 1945 novel Animal Farm in school. I distinctly remember being as enchanted by the talking animals as I was inspired by the power of metaphor and allegory. Could literature actually do that? Could it weave something magically spellbinding while critiquing society at the same time? My own teenager unequivocally declared Animal Farm, was her favorite novel in middle school. Though many years have passed since those early days of falling in love with books, I still seek that thrill of discovery, that leap of the heart that happens when I’m captivated by a story. It’s even better when a wide audience of readers shares the experience with me. To those of us elated by Animal Farm, my dedicated teacher in the Memphis public schools said 1984 was the next novel by Orwell that we should read, though it was far less often assigned. I didn’t read it until graduate school, and I remember thinking about how it resembled and differed from Animal Farm. In both novels Orwell’s satiric voice veers between cautionary and caustic, but in 1984 his dystopian vision had deepened, his perspective broadened. If Animal Farm was a specific critique of the events leading up to the Russian Revolution, 1984 expanded into a more wide-ranging criticism of what might happen if a totalitarian government took complete control. That layered complexity has given Orwell’s last published novel “legs,” as some might put it. Since its publication seventy-five years ago, it has inspired innumerable essays analyzing everything from the three slogans of the Party—War is Peace, Freedom is Slavery, Ignorance is Strength—to its predictions about the death of language and ideas. It is most certainly a testament to Orwell’s accomplishment that the novel has fruitfully inspired nearly a century of close readings. Recently, however, I read 1984 alone, without the benefits of a classroom setting. I wanted to imagine myself as a new reader. How might I feel about this book if I didn’t know it as a classic text? What if I wandered into the bookstore and picked it up because I thought the premise was intriguing? I know, I know. This feels like an impossible hypothetical. Everyone knows 1984 is canonical. Yet when I asked around recently, most of my friends admitted that they’d either never read the novel or hadn’t read it in many years. So perhaps this idea isn’t as far-fetched as it sounds. Let’s try it. Let’s enter the Orwellian universe as if for the first time. I pick up the book and begin to read the first pages. When the novel opens, Winston Smith has been summoned to help a neighbor unclog her sink in their decaying apartment building ironically named Victory Mansions. Though he is only thirty-nine years old, we learn that he has a varicose ulcer on his leg. He lives alone and works for the government. The details feel banal, quotidian. But then this ordinariness is immediately shot through with weirdness: there are two-way telescreens everywhere, and Winston must meticulously guard his thoughts and movements or he could be apprehended by the Thought Police. The Thought Police? There is something wildly imaginative about these opening pages, and I am both intrigued and horrified. In an era of nearly ubiquitous cameras and facial recognition technology and social media. I am no stranger to the loss of privacy. But Orwell’s portrayal of thought surveillance boggles the mind. He writes that “even a back can be revealing.” To add to this terror, Winston is guilty of more than just a thoughtcrime\ he has written down his heresy. I must keep reading to find out more. But, first, I do something I often do when I’m a chapter or two into a book. I flip to the back cover and read the details again. The book was published in 1949, but the novel is set in 1984. thirty-five years later. I glance at the author’s biographical details and learn that Orwell was dead by 1950. Remember. I am imagining myself encountering the book for the first time. I am just realizing that Orwell died at forty-six years old. Had he lived to a not-unreasonable eighty-one, he would have been able to witness firsthand which path the world would take by 1984. I understand in those opening pages that I am reading a dystopian novel, an imagined future in which government surveillance constricts and defines people’s lives. It’s a strange orientation because I am reading it at a time beyond 1984 and can therefore measure what Orwell guessed correctly about the future while also noting his contemporaneous perspective. Orwell presciently addresses his conundrum in the first chapter. “How could you communicate with the future? It was of its nature impossible. Either the future would resemble the present in which case it would not listen to him. or it would be different from it, and his predicament would be meaningless.” Yet I would argue that it is precisely because of the novel’s longevity that he manages to speak to the future. And its longevity is partially due to his prescience. I write historical novels, which means I spend a lot of time in library archives. Examining old letters or maps or diaries transports me. Once you’ve experienced this, you know that history is not really past. We can relive historical moments, a feeling that is nothing short of mystical. I think the same is true of the future. In dystopian fiction, writers journey into their imagined worlds. Orwell speaks to us because his imagination allowed him to move through time. Writers (and readers!) are true time travelers with access to the portal. Now that Orwell has established this ordinary but weird world, one not entirely dissimilar to my own, I begin to connect to the humans who populate it. There is the Inner Party, the Outer Party, and the proles. Our unsettled protagonist Winston Smith is a member of the Outer Party, but he has already begun to dissociate himself from the propaganda of the government by writing down his thoughts. I sense that the heat of dramatic tension will lie in Winston’s burgeoning discontent. It’s a great start. I’m enjoying the novel on its own terms, not as a classic but as a good story; that is, until Winston reveals himself to be a problematic character. For example, we learn of him: “He disliked nearly all women, and especially the young and pretty ones.” Whoa, wait a minute, Orwell. Winston’s views on women are, at first, despicable to the contemporary reader. He is the kind of character who can make me put a book down. When I was younger, that’s exactly what I would have done. But I’m a more seasoned reader now’, and I know the difference between a flawed character and a flawed story. And I remind myself that this is a dystopian novel, an idea of what society might look like if certain dark forces prevail. Orwell is suggesting misogyny is likely in a totalitarian society, and Winston is a product of that environment. Naturally, the women characters are also affected by totalitarianism. Under the Party’s rule, the sole purpose of marriage is to produce children. Katharine, Winston’s estranged wife, is diligently committed to that principle, but she despises the duty, and they remain childless. Julia, a twenty-six-year-old who works in the Fiction Department, takes the initiative to seduce Winston; unlike Katharine, she has reclaimed her sexuality as something more than a means to reproduce. Julia fervently believes the best way to rebel against the Party is by these small acts of individualism. That individualism is also on display in the tireless singing of the laundry woman in the courtyard behind Winston’s rented room. To Winston, her singing is delightful and brightens the dismal scene. Her ability to find joy in a mundane existence is deeply affecting to him, and he concludes from this joy that she must be beautiful. Luckily for us, Winston evolves as his love for Julia grows. Though he struggles with sincere emotion, because for so many years the Party has deprived its citizens of passion, he still manages to fall in love with her. By reconnecting him to his suppressed emotions, Julia teaches him there is a part of himself that the Party cannot reach. At this point I feel glad I’ve continued with the story. Orwell is suggesting that love and artistic beauty can act as healing forces in a totalitarian state. I think of my own love for literature, the ways in which my lifelong passion for reading has healed me on many occasions. I think of my love for family, friends, and community, and I am invested in the story again. I am turning pages. I wouldn’t say that I identify with these themes of human connection because they are universal. I am of the generation that pushed back against notions of the universal., especially when they weren’t universal at all and applied only to a particular kind of experience. I am a Black female reader, and these identifiers are primary points of entry into any text for me. Not that every book I love must contain a character who looks or thinks like me; I have learned to do what many readers on the margins have learned to do: read around the margins. In other words, I examine the contours of a novel like an outline that I can trace, to find connection to the story even in the tiniest details. And Orwell’s nods to the possibilities of love and pleasure are an outline I can trace over and over. That sliver of connection can be difficult for someone like me to find in a novel that does not speak much to race and ethnicity at all. In Oceania, there is supposedly no racism. “Nor is there any racial discrimination, or any marked domination of one province by another. Jews. Negroes, South Americans of pure Indian blood are to be found in the highest ranks of the Party, and administrators of any area are always drawn from the inhabitants of that area. In no part of Oceania do the inhabitants have the feeling they are a colonial population ruled from a distant capital.” When I read this, I cannot help but think of Ralph Ellison’s Invisible Man and its publication in the United States just a year after 1984 was published in Britain. In Ellison’s novel, whites don’t see Blacks, while in Orwell’s novel, there are no Black characters at all. As a contemporary reader I find myself pausing again. It is plausible that there is no racism and colonialism in Orwell’s world since the totalitarian government has erased and rewritten history numerous times in an effort to portray the government in a positive light. But Orwell suggests it is impossible to completely ignore these “secret” histories. In his first diary entry at the beginning of the novel, Winston writes of seeing a war film in which a woman who is possibly a “jewess” sits among refugees in a lifeboat—a possible reference to Holocaust refugees. In a 1945 essay. “Antisemitism in Britain.” Orwell frankly criticizes antisemitism among his British contemporaries, but in other documents he is guilty of the very antisemitic remarks that he disapprovingly notes in others. Despite these contradictions. I am willing to accept that Orwell wants to center other concerns, and I dip back into Winston’s world. As a storyteller. Orwell provides a satisfying ending, and though I am finished. I find myself flipping back through the book, rereading passages. This is the kind of book that one must digest, a book that I want to discuss with someone. I may not physically be in the classroom, but I am. A classroom of my own making. Again, I am struck by how the pleasure of reading is best shared with others. Even as I read through a contemporary lens without the benefit of a teacher guiding me, I am connected to this Orwellian world because it still offers so much to contemplate. In this rereading, I am struck by the state’s control of women’s bodies, the oppression of the masses, the fates of people of color, and the erasure of language. I think of the many dystopian novels that have been published since 1984, novels such as Parable of the Sower by Octavia E. Butler, Never Let Me Go by Kazuo Ishiguro, The Road by Cormac McCarthy, or The Handmaid's Tale by Margaret Atwood. Each of these writers offers a critique of society that has a powerful pull not only on our imaginations, but also on our sense of self. Who are we and what are the implications of our actions? Because of its ability to hold both story and ideas in the palm of its hand, 1984 was a joyful reread for me, even with its imperfections. In this rereading. I considered the book’s larger intentions while also asking a basic question: Is it a good story? I tried to recapture the wonder of a child encountering Orwell for the first time, and in that, I probably failed. It is impossible to do so when I no longer possess the innocence of youth. I am now more firmly grounded in reading history and in a set of expectations. Now. when I pick up a book, I bring my own story to it. Furthermore, the book is too imprinted in our collective consciousness, too many of its references used in other contexts. Big Brother. Ministry of Truth. Two plus two equals five. Thought Police. Newspeak. Orwell’s ideas have permeated popular culture. This book has pushed me to think about love and community as healing forces, as powerful modes of resistance. Although the nature of dystopian novels is that they do not typically embrace such optimism. I tend to agree with Margaret Atwood’s observation that because the coda at the end of the book is written in the past tense, it suggests that the government does not win. If the government does not ultimately win, that means the people are more powerful than we know. I am back to the wonder of discovering Animal Farm, back to rejoicing at the power of literature to weave a spell and craft a vision at the same time. Somehow I have managed to discover a way to enter 1984 seventy-five years after its initial publication and find new appreciation for it, new love for it. Yes. I have said it. I loved so much about this book, and I understand its lasting impact. So I suppose, in the end, I have succeeded in recapturing that initial thrill of discovering the possibilities of literature. —Dolen Perkins-Valdez
